rows.text: A comparison of the measure-valued proposal with the partial-possibility logic should test whether the former can reproduce the latter’s consequence behavior; their different semantic-value formats alone do not establish incompatibility.

A semantics of the dialogue in (37) must distinguish the “Almost certainly” reply from a simple epistemic-possibility utterance, rather than infer the reply’s interpretation from an account of simple epistemic modals.

Assessment sensitivity and BEM indeterminacy are distinct explanatory dimensions: the former concerns whether truth varies with the context of assessment, while the latter concerns which group's information is relevant. Adopting one therefore does not by itself refute the other.

Epistemic modals can quantify over possible worlds at the operator level, while the alternative-semantics claim applies at least to the analyzed “probably” utterance in dialogue (37b); it need not deny possible-world quantification generally.
Epistemic modals can quantify over possible worlds without every sentence containing an epistemic modal expressing possible-worlds content.
Even if the dynamic approach is favored for its predictions about quantified sentences, that evidence alone does not displace the ortholattice account of genuine epistemic contradictions.
For epistemic modals, truth-conditionality and absolute truth are distinct commitments: assessment-relative truth conditions can preserve the former without the latter.

For epistemic possibility, passing the communicative-objection test for relativist semantics and favoring the informational view for pragmatics and informational consequence are compatible assessments of different criteria; success on the former does not by itself rule out the latter.

For epistemic-modal knowledge claims, information available to a later assessor can bear on whether the earlier claim meets worldly-information safety, but does not replace the information determined at nearby worlds; assessment-sensitive retraction norms govern whether retraction is required.
In the “Almost certainly” exchange, the reply should update interlocutors’ shared probabilistic information about whether Liem is wearing green, rather than assert a possible-worlds proposition.
In the “Almost certainly” exchange, the reply’s simple epistemic use should be analyzed as nonfactual coordination between interlocutors, not as a factual report of the speaker’s information.

Information-sensitive Safety is compatible with unrestricted second constructive dilemma leading to bad results: a condition on knowledge of epistemic modal claims can hold while that inference form requires restriction.
Interpreting “Almost certainly” as a reply to “Is Liem probably wearing green?” requires an account of probabilistic replies beyond an account restricted to simple epistemic modals.

Knowledge of epistemic modals and the validity of inferences involving modal premises require distinct assessments: satisfying an information-sensitive knowledge condition does not by itself license an unrestricted constructive-dilemma inference.

rows.text: Motivational support for alternatives to contextualism does not by itself establish relativist semantics as the best account of epistemic-modal thought and talk; that case requires empirical assessment.

Success in explaining quantified epistemic-modal defects is a distinct criterion from making epistemic contradictions genuine; support for the dynamic direction on the quantified challenge does not by itself answer the contradiction criterion.

The BEM approach’s use of standard context-dependent semantics and indeterminacy about the relevant information group is a competing explanation of epistemic modals, not a literal negation of assessment-sensitive truth.

The Moss probability-measure proposal and the von Fintel–Gillies account should be treated as distinct architectures, not as a demonstrated contradiction: the former assigns probability-measure sets to epistemic expressions including indicative conditionals, while the latter’s stated account concerns bare epistemic modals and explains their behavior through context dependence and pragmatics. This qualified distinction does not establish that either architecture supersedes or is equivalent to the other.

The comparison should be restricted by expression class: the probability-measure proposal covers epistemic modals and indicative conditionals, whereas the indeterminacy and context-dependent-pragmatics claims at issue concern bare epistemic modals. The latter claims therefore do not settle whether the former proposal is appropriate for indicative conditionals.

The dynamic direction’s support concerning quantified epistemic-modal phenomena does not by itself settle the contradiction behavior of epistemic-modal formulas; that behavior requires separate assessment, including against the ortholattice approach.

The epistemic consequence relation and the type of semantic values assigned to epistemic sentences are distinct dimensions; a possibility-based account and a measure-based proposal need not be rival answers on a single axis.

The resistance of epistemic modals to standard truth-conditional frameworks concerns frameworks requiring absolute truth values; assessment-sensitive truth conditions remain viable without absolute truth values.
The semantic-value question addressed by expressivism and the question whether epistemic-modal truth varies with the assessor are distinct explananda, not competing answers to one question.
The “Almost certainly” reply should be interpreted as coordinating interlocutors on their information, rather than as expressing a possible-worlds proposition.
World quantification by epistemic modals is compatible with a non-possible-worlds semantics for Moss’s analyzed “probably” dialogue.

rows.text: A later assessor should require retraction of an earlier epistemic-modal knowledge claim only when it fails information-sensitive safety relative to the worldly information at nearby worlds relevant to that claim; such a failure, rather than mere disagreement, supplies the retraction basis.

A proposal's use of standard context-dependent semantic machinery does not by itself show that epistemic-modal truth is independent of the assessor; thus that methodological advantage alone does not settle whether assessment sensitivity is needed.

An adequate account of epistemic-modal retraction must specify how worldly information at nearby worlds bears on knowledge safety and how retraction norms apply across assessment contexts; neither condition alone establishes the link.

An assessment-sensitive retraction of an epistemic-modal knowledge claim is warranted only when the claim fails the nearby-world worldly-information safety condition; a later assessor's disagreement alone is insufficient.

Assessment-relative truth for epistemic-modal claims is compatible with indeterminacy about which group's information a bare modal quantifies over: assessor-relative evaluation need not determine a unique information group, and group indeterminacy need not eliminate assessor-sensitive truth.
Communicative adequacy for relativist epistemic-modal semantics and intuitive support for informational pragmatics are distinct explananda: success on the former does not test the latter.
Contextually supplied perspective restrictors do not by themselves determine a unique group of investigators whose aggregated information fixes the interpretation of a bare epistemic modal.

Epistemic modal quantification over possible worlds is compatible with probability expressions such as “probably” lacking possible-worlds contents, because those claims concern different semantic levels.
Epistemic modals can quantify over possible worlds without probability expressions embedded under epistemic vocabulary expressing possible-worlds content.
For epistemic modals, relativism is better supported than Solipsistic Contextualism when both genuine-dispute cases and the communicative objection are considered.

In epistemic-modal semantics, indeterminacy over which group's information is relevant concerns parameter selection, whereas assessment sensitivity concerns how a claim's truth is evaluated; neither thesis alone settles the other's question.
In probability-question dialogue, a reply such as “Almost certainly” functions as an evidential comment on the prejacent, rather than as an assertion of the prejacent’s truth.
In the cited dialogue, “Almost certainly” answers the probability question at the level of the likelihood assigned to the prejacent; it does not assert the prejacent itself.

Moss’s probability-measure proposal concerns the semantic values assigned to epistemic expressions, whereas von Fintel and Gillies’s account concerns indeterminate group-information selection for bare epistemic modals. Their commitments warrant comparing these distinct dimensions, but do not establish that the approaches are incompatible, equivalent, or exhaustive alternatives.

rows.text: Moss’s probability-measure semantics for epistemic expressions and von Fintel and Gillies’s account of indeterminate group information for bare epistemic modals address distinct architectural questions. The bounded review supports only a qualified comparison: later work offers partial treatments, but the evidence establishes neither incompatibility, equivalence, supersession, nor an exhaustive current-open verdict.

On the stated claims, a possibility-based account of epistemic-modal consequence and a proposal to use sets of probability measures as semantic values address different formal questions; their difference alone does not establish incompatibility.

Surviving the communicative objection does not settle whether the informational view of epistemic-modal pragmatics is preferable: the former concerns communicative adequacy, while the latter concerns intuitive support for an informational view.

The fact that epistemic modals quantify over possible worlds does not determine whether a sentence containing “probably” expresses possible-worlds content; in the dialogue case, an alternative semantics is needed.

The grounds for pursuing alternatives to contextualism about epistemic modals and an account’s success in explaining genuine disputes about what might be the case are independent criteria; motivation to pursue alternatives does not by itself establish that an alternative explains those disputes.
The “Almost certainly” reply in probability-question dialogue is best analyzed as an evidential comment within a measure-valued semantics, rather than as an ordinary possible-worlds assertion.
